rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window for all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing truncation risk. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient duration to test how much of the substantial resolution margin can be traded for speed. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness.

Test the upper temperature limit at the faster gradient to shift selectivity in the unresolved central cluster and shorten retention further. This comparison isolates temperature effects before refining gradient duration.

Test an intermediate temperature to balance the central-cluster separation against the new close pair seen at 60 C. The 10-minute gradient should retain the zero time penalty while mapping this selectivity tradeoff.

At 55 C, the central close pair may reach baseline resolution before the pair approaching co-elution at 60 C becomes too compressed. Keep the fast gradient fixed to test this selectivity balance without adding a time penalty.

Test a steeper gradient at 50 C: the temperature-driven order change suggests it may open the remaining close pair, while the other pairs retain some resolution margin. This also preserves the zero time penalty.

A slightly shallower gradient should improve the limiting pair at 55 C, while the other close pair may remain near baseline resolution. The last peak should still elute near the zero-time-penalty window.

Injection 7 already reached the maximum CRF. This method preserves its gradient slope and temperature but trims the unused high-organic segment; all peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining the same separation and score.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test whether raising the starting organic fraction can shorten retention while preserving full resolution. Keeping gradient slope and temperature fixed isolates the starting-composition effect.

Slightly flatten the gradient to recover resolution of the limiting pair at the higher starting organic fraction. This may preserve the maximum CRF with a larger resolution margin while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes.

The maximum score is secured; a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 may improve its limiting resolution while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes. The 0.60 endpoint should still place all peaks inside the gradient.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a compensating shallower slope to preserve the critical-pair separation. This may maintain the maximum CRF with improved resolution margin and last-peak elution near 8 minutes.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore the low-temperature selectivity regime for another fully resolved, fast method. Cooling may separate the central cluster in the opposite elution order, although other pairs could become limiting.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 60 C separates the pair that crossed elution order near this temperature, potentially yielding a faster maximum-score method. The established CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmark.

Refine near injection 7 with a slightly shallower gradient to improve its 1.59-resolution pair while checking that the other critical pair remains above 1.5. Last-peak elution should remain close to 8 minutes, potentially preserving the maximum CRF.

Explore the opposite side of the high-temperature elution-order crossover by raising the starting organic fraction. This may open the pair that nearly co-eluted at 60 C and provide a faster maximum-score alternative; monitor early-peak retention and the central cluster.

Raise the starting organic fraction one more step at the same slope to test whether the remaining close pair separates beyond the crossover. This could shorten the run further, but the first two peaks must be checked for excessive compression near the dead time.

Return to the lower starting fraction to restore early-pair resolution, then steepen the gradient to move the central pair farther beyond its crossover. This tests a faster alternative while retaining the established maximum-score methods as the benchmark.

Reduce the slope relative to injection 12 to recover its limiting pair while testing whether the higher starting fraction provides a larger overall resolution margin. This may incur a small time penalty; the established CRF 1.000 methods remain optimal for the stated score.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 19 to bring its remaining critical pair above 1.5 while retaining the other pair’s resolution margin. The last peak is expected near 9 minutes, testing whether this alternative can also achieve the maximum CRF without a time penalty.

Probe a slightly shallower slope than injection 11 to map the maximum-score plateau at the moderate starting composition. The limiting central pair should remain near baseline resolution, with the last peak expected below 9 minutes.

Use a slope between injections 11 and 21, both of which achieved the maximum CRF, to refine the fully resolved operating region. This should retain baseline separation of both critical pairs and keep the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

Test a trimmed solvent window with a slope between the maximum-score methods from injections 21 and 22. Both critical pairs should remain above 1.5, with all compounds eluting during the gradient and no time penalty.

Preserve injection 11’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while extending the high-organic endpoint. Because all peaks eluted before the earlier gradient ended, this should retain its maximum CRF and approximately 1.58 minimum resolution.

Finish with an untested grid method that preserves injection 7’s starting composition, gradient slope, and temperature while trimming the unused endpoint. All peaks should elute during the gradient, reproducing the maximum CRF of 1.000 and last-peak time near 7.60 minutes.
